gist: Atwood identifies the universal Spirit, as first revealed in human life, with the mesmeric agent and the Alchemists' despised subject. She says the purification of this subject and of the understanding was the purpose of the ancient Purificative Rites. She presents the Hermetic art as the purification of this passive, undetermined middle substance, by itself, into the Stone, a work that only a laboring philosopher can achieve.

notes.point: Aristotle's passive intellect is the Mundane Spirit as first revealed in humanity: convertible to any inclination, truth or delusion, manifesting motives in vital effects.
It is the agent of present-day mesmerizing, the New Imponderable, being the Common Soul; and the Alchemists' abject subject-matter, converted to every will.
The world disesteems it unknowingly; who knows the Art and has the medium will be richest.
Naturally, the microcosmic life resembles the world's vitality breathed into the blood; it needs melioration; in this Door-keeper Isis is not revealed.

This is only the Labyrinth's gate, where the human spirit's similitudes lure adventurers into Magic. The Eternal Riddle is the Compound Simple; Hercules' Augean labor is to turn life's current into another channel and purify its source.

In the Mysteries, Purificative Rites followed the Medial Life's revealment, restoring reason's monarchy before the final initiations. She dwells on this first step and the need of intellectual preparation.
Objections: inner revelation lacks witness and is biased; nothing universal is observed; why is omnipresent Being unperceived?
Reply: sense draws the light outward, forgetting its source; turned inward, impediments removed, it might reveal the antecedent life, unless the understanding is too polluted (Bacon).
Passive dreaming in the phantasy is perilous; before contemplation all else must be obliterated and the mind made clear and passive.
Mystic philosophy hinges on purifying the Understanding Essence and making its occult Causality conscious; doubt concerns means, not possibility of self-knowledge.
The Hermetic and Eleusinian purifications truly perfected human life, by means purer than Mesmerism's; the ancients began by purifying the Vital Spirit in its proper Light.
This seeming nothing, solved, resolved and manipulated, becomes the concrete Stone: a mirror of nature's reason and medium of divine experience.
Draw the least thing into the ferment; the metal is outwardly dead, inwardly alive; collect what philosophers prize; remove superfluities.
Art cannot change the perfect or perfect the utterly imperfect; the Universal Spirit is a passive middle substance, self-purifying, agent and patient: the Sun and Moon philosophical.
The art takes this Undetermined Subject where nature leaves her, through amalgamation, distillation, filtration, digestion and sublimation, into a new concentric Form of Light.
Nature has one secret agent, distinct through numberless species by their seeds.
Only philosophers laboring rationally see the Keystone restored; the idle, vicious and foolish are excluded; none imparts what he lacks.

method.veiled: which Aristotle, in his Metaphysics, calls passive intellect, because capable of receiving and being converted to all
method.plain: The universal Mundane Spirit, as it first becomes conscious in human life, is a receptive intellect. It takes on whatever it receives, good or bad, true or delusive, and shows motives in vital effects.
method.basis: II.2 ¶17 says why it is called passive intellect.

also.text: the best pr worst inclination, the highest truth or the most delusive imaginings

method.veiled: the identical agent which is spread abroad in the present day mesmerizing, the photogenic medium, our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul
method.plain: The agent at work in mesmerism is this same receptive Spirit, the Common Soul.
method.basis: II.2 ¶18 asserts the identity directly.

method.veiled: a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands
method.plain: The Alchemists' despised, common subject-matter is this same Common Soul. It is present everywhere, unrecognized, and turned unconsciously to any will.
method.basis: II.2 ¶18: 'also the subject-matter of the Alchemists aforesaid', in the same sentence as the identification with the Common Soul.

also.text: moving here below in shadowy manifestation, invisibly and unconsciously converted to every will and various use
It is what the world cares not for, as the adept says, but disesteems it; it hath it in its sight, carries it in its hands, yet is ignorant thereof

method.veiled: he that knows the Art, and the expressions, and hath the medium, will be richer than any other
method.plain: Success needs three things: knowledge of the Art, understanding of its (veiled) expressions, and possession of the medium.
method.basis: II.2 ¶18. 'the medium' is read as the subject just described, which ¶18 calls 'the photogenic medium'.

method.veiled: the microcosmic life is not dissimilar from the vitality of the greater world, which is included by respiration in the blood of all creatures
method.plain: In its natural state, the life in the individual is like the world's general vitality: breathing takes it into the blood, and it pulses in flux and reflux. In this state it needs improvement.
method.basis: II.2 ¶18 states the likeness and adds 'how much such a life is in need of melioration'.

also.text: how much such a life is in need of melioration

method.veiled: that in her Door-keeper, Isis is not revealed
method.plain: The life's first, natural manifestation does not reveal its full nature. That manifestation is only the threshold.
method.basis: II.2 ¶18: the preceding clause says this life falls short and needs melioration. II.2 ¶19: 'so far we have yet advanced only to the gate'. See ambiguities.

method.veiled: the Sphinx is even now present, rapidly propounding her dark riddles in the world, images of the obscure and intricate nature of the human spirit
method.plain: The human spirit's own windings, attractions and resemblances mislead whoever enters it. They draw such people into magic, where many go astray.
method.basis: II.2 ¶19 glosses the riddles as images of the human spirit and describes the luring.

also.text: into that Hermetic wilderness and wild of Magic in which so many adventurers have gone astray

method.veiled: This is the Monster and the Eternal Riddle explained to common sense as suits it, but misunderstood to this day; that Compound Simple and ground of the magians’ elements
method.plain: The subject is one essence that contains everything, yet is divided off in each particular thing. That is why the magians described it so confusingly.
method.basis: II.2 ¶19: 'an essence all comprehending, yet separated in each particular, by so great an interval from itself'.

also.text: an essence all comprehending, yet separated in each particular, by so great an interval from itself

method.veiled: But this is that Augean Stable that was to be cleansed, that most famous labor of the philosophic Hercules
method.plain: The great labor is to redirect the flow of life and purify its natural source.
method.basis: II.2 ¶19 glosses the labor: 'to turn the current of life into another channel, and purify the natural source'.

also.text: to turn the current of life into another channel, and purify the natural source

method.veiled: Close upon the revealment of the Medial Life then, as we take it, in order of the Mysteries followed the Purificative Rites, which were designed also to restore the monarchy of reason in the soul
method.plain: After the Medial Life is revealed, the next step is purification, which puts reason back in rule over the soul. This is preparation for the final initiations, not the end.

also.text: not either as an end so much, but as preparatory to undergoing the final initiations

method.veiled: that very light is drawn outwardly, and enchanted by sense that it is internally unconscious and oblivious everywhere of the great Identity whence it springs
method.plain: True Being is present but not perceived because attention is drawn outward through the senses. It therefore cannot perceive its own source.
method.basis: II.2 ¶21 gives this as the answer to the objection in II.2 ¶20.

method.veiled: If that were applied inwardly which now looks out, and every natural impediment removed, experience might then reveal to us the antecedent life
method.plain: Turn the outward-looking faculty inward and remove natural impediments. Then experience may reveal the prior source-life.

method.veiled: if by this traditionary fall and outbirth, the understanding is so polluted as to be no more able, as Lord Bacon supposes (17), to reflect the total reason to itself
method.plain: If the understanding is too corrupted to reflect reason, introspection is useless. Atwood treats this as a possibility that must be tested.
method.basis: II.2 ¶21: 'introspection will be useless'; it 'behooves us to consider scrupulously ... the possibility and tests'.

method.veiled: who trust themselves to remain passively dreaming in the region of the phantasy, with its notions and instincts, often more false, fleeting, and evil that the corporeal images with which sense is conversant
method.plain: Passively wandering in the imagination is dangerous. Its contents are often falser than ordinary sense impressions.

method.veiled: that all else be effectually obliterated, and the mental atmosphere made clear and passive before its objective light. Without this, they promise nothing; with it, all.
method.plain: Before contemplation, everything else must be cleared from the mind. The mind must become clear and receptive before the light of Reason. This is the indispensable precondition.
method.basis: II.2 ¶22: 'before any one betakes himself to the inner life of contemplation --- before he hopes, we mean, to pass into its Reason'.

method.veiled: namely, of purifying the human Understanding Essence, and developing to consciousness its occult Causality
method.plain: The mystics' whole philosophy depends on two things: purifying the understanding and bringing its hidden causal power into consciousness.

also.text: the doubt rather remains also about the discovery of means, than the possibility of self-knowledge

method.veiled: were real and efficacious for the highest ends that philosophy can propose to itself, namely, the purification and perfection of human life
method.plain: The aim of the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries was to purify and perfect human life. Their means were higher than those of mesmerism.

also.text: the administration in proportion purer, holier, and entirely scientific

method.veiled: purifying the Vital Spirit in its proper Light
method.plain: The ancients began from where modern experiment ends: purifying the vital spirit. The chunk does not further define 'its proper Light'.

method.veiled: it is the very same which solved and resolved, and wisely manipulated, becomes to be the concrete Stone of philosophers
method.plain: The Stone is this same subtle principle, worked on by repeated solution and skilled handling. In its pure, passive state it mirrors universal reason and mediates divine experience.

also.text: in its pure, passive expanse, a mirror of the catholic reason of nature, and the medium of that holy and sublime experience granted to man alone in the divine alliance

method.veiled: Take that which is least, and draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers
method.plain: Begin with the most despised, least-valued thing and bring it by art into fermentation. This chunk does not explain what the ferment is.
method.basis: II.2 ¶26. 'that which is least' is read alongside the 'abject' subject of II.2 ¶18.

method.veiled: although our metal is exteriorly dead, yet it has life within
method.plain: The subject looks inert from outside but holds an inner life.

method.veiled: only in the preparation removing superfluities
method.plain: Preparation means separation: keep what the philosopher values, discard what most people value, and remove what is superfluous. The garbled preceding words seem to say that nothing else is added or taken away.
method.basis: II.2 ¶26: 'That which in the eyes of a philosopher is the most precious should be collected, and that That which the many set more value on be rejected'. See ambiguities for the corrupt phrase.

also.text: That which in the eyes of a philosopher is the most precious should be collected, and that That which the many set more value on be rejected

method.veiled: but this Universal Spirit is described as a middle substance --- passive, undetermined, susceptible of conversion and all extremes
method.plain: Only something between the perfect and the utterly imperfect can be perfected by art. This Spirit is such an undetermined middle thing.
method.basis: II.2 ¶26: 'From that which is perfect nothing more can be made ... neither from an utterly imperfect thing can art produce perfection'.

also.text: From that which is perfect nothing more can be made; for a perfect species is not changed in its nature, neither from an utterly imperfect thing can art produce perfection

method.veiled: the one thing requisite, purifying and to be purified itself by itself, in turn agent and patient, which are the Hermetic luminaries
method.plain: The single subject purifies itself: it is both what acts and what is acted on. Its active and passive sides are the 'luminaries', the philosophical Sun and Moon. As the work advances, they pass through many phases from imperfection to perfection.
method.basis: II.2 ¶26 identifies agent and patient with the Hermetic luminaries, the Sun and Moon philosophical.

also.text: in their full representative advancement, the Sun and Moon philosophical, passing through many phases from imperfection to perfection in the true magistery

method.veiled: the hermetic art would seem to consist simply in the right disposition and manipulation of this our Undetermined Subject, taking her where nature leaves
method.plain: The art is the correct handling of this undetermined subject. It picks up where natural development stops.

method.veiled: as of amalgamation, distillation, filtration, digestion, and lastly by sublimation to the Head of an appropriate Vessel
method.plain: The operations, in the order listed, are amalgamation, distillation, filtration, digestion and finally sublimation. This chunk does not explain them; they are 'to be hereafter noted'.
method.basis: II.2 ¶27 lists the operations only.

method.veiled: establishing her in a new and concentric Form of Light
method.plain: The end of the operations is the subject established in a new and concentric Form of Light. This chunk does not explain it further.

method.veiled: For she her secret agent doth possess, Which in the universe is only one, But is distinct thro’ species numberless, According to their seeds
method.plain: Nature has one secret agent, one in the universe but distinct through numberless species according to their seeds. The verse also says the life of things is a hidden light, discerned by soaring minds.
method.basis: II.2 ¶28 verse.

also.text: Their life is light which in them hidden lies, Discerned by the eyes of soaring minds

method.veiled: None but a philosopher ever achieved the work, or for reasons that are imperative, ever will.
method.plain: Only a true philosopher can do the work. The idle, the vicious and fools without the principle of improvement in themselves are excluded. One can impart only what one has, and one has it only by laboring rationally.

also.text: The idle and vicious are totally excluded, nor are the rewards of Wisdom to be won by fools wanting the very principles of melioration in themselves
He only that hath it can impart --- and he only has it who has labored rationally in the pursuit
The earth giveth much mould, whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of

method.veiled: all the labors of that Heroic Intellect to be passed through before the rejected Keystone regains her Head place
method.plain: The work is completed only after long intellectual labor. This chunk does not decode the 'rejected Keystone' (see ambiguities).
method.basis: II.2 ¶29. The possible readings are drawn from II.2 ¶18, ¶20 and ¶27.

ambiguities.quote: that in her Door-keeper, Isis is not revealed
readings: The natural, first-manifested life (the 'Door-keeper') does not reveal Isis, i.e. the full nature of what it guards.
The present-day mesmeric manifestation of the agent falls short of the full mystery.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: the same sentence of II.2 ¶18 on the natural life's need of melioration. Reading 2: II.2 ¶18 identifies the mesmeric agent with the subject, II.2 ¶19 says 'so far we have yet advanced only to the gate', and II.2 ¶24 calls the object of the Mysteries superior to Mesmerism's.

ambiguities.quote: Close upon the revealment of the Medial Life then
readings: The Medial Life is the Mundane Spirit or Common Soul as first revealed, described in ¶17–19.
The Medial Life is a stage in the order of the Mysteries that this chunk does not otherwise identify.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: 'then' links back to the preceding paragraphs; II.2 ¶17 speaks of the Spirit 'as it is at first consciously revealed'; II.2 ¶26 calls the Universal Spirit 'a middle substance'. Reading 2: no explicit identity is stated.

ambiguities.quote: That which is, in his mind, so mere a nothing, become sin that of a philosopher to be the All in all
readings: 'become sin that' is an error for 'becomes in that': what is nothing in his mind becomes in the philosopher's mind the All in all.
The text is corrupt and its exact wording is uncertain.
ambiguities.basis: The sense of the contrast between 'his mind' and 'that of a philosopher' in II.2 ¶25.

ambiguities.quote: O, how wonderful different and detract nothing, only in the preparation removing superfluities
readings: Preparation adds nothing different and takes nothing away except superfluities.
The passage is garbled and its sense cannot be recovered beyond 'removing superfluities'.
ambiguities.basis: The surrounding words in II.2 ¶26 on collecting what is precious and rejecting what the many value.

ambiguities.quote: before the rejected Keystone regains her Head place
readings: The despised subject is restored to supremacy at the completion of the work.
Reason is restored to rule in the soul.
The subject is raised by sublimation to the Head of the Vessel.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: II.2 ¶18 (the subject is disesteemed and 'abject'). Reading 2: II.2 ¶20 ('restore the monarchy of reason in the soul'). Reading 3: II.2 ¶27 ('sublimation to the Head of an appropriate Vessel'); the feminine 'her' matches 'taking her where nature leaves' in ¶27.

translations.original: Ex natura et divino factum est
translations.translation: It is made from nature and the divine.

translations.original: Divinum enim quia cum divinitate conjunctum divinas substantias facit.
translations.translation: For it is divine because, joined with divinity, it makes divine substances.

translations.original: Nemo enim dat id, quod non habet.
translations.translation: He only that hath it can impart

translations.original: Non levis adscensus, si quis petat ardua, sudor Plurimus hunc tollit, nocturna insomnis olivae Immoritur, delet quod mox laudaverit in se, Qui cupit aeternae donari frondis honore.
translations.translation: The ascent is not light. If anyone seeks the heights, much sweat raises him; sleepless, he wears himself out over the nightly olive-lamp and erases in himself what he will soon have praised, whoever desires to be granted the honour of the eternal leaf.

threads.note: 'All which we understand' refers back to the preceding discussion, which is not in this chunk.
'the Alchemists aforesaid' points to Alchemists cited earlier.
'as we proceed to unfold the ultimate tradition of this Wisdom' and 'the final initiations' point to later treatment of the final initiations.
'some mother grounds hereafter to be disposed of' promises later grounds for the inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious.
The particulars of the means employed in the Mysteries 'are further discussed under the Practice'.
The 'divers operations' (amalgamation, distillation, filtration, digestion, sublimation) are 'to be hereafter noted'.
